terms.gloss: bias, partisanship, favour for one side
evidence: Tac. Ann. 1.1: sine īrā et studiō
terms.comment: Its ordinary senses are zeal, eagerness, interest and study; as bias it is the eagerness that takes a side, studium partium, party spirit (Cic. Verr. 2.1.35, Lewis & Short). Tacitus promises to write sine īrā et studiō, without anger and without bias.
An opinion formed before the facts are heard. nē quid praejūdicātī afferātis, “bring no prejudice with you” (Cic. Clu. 6).

terms.gloss: biased, partial (of a judge or witness)
evidence: Cic. Font. 21: cupidī et īrātī et conjūrātī testēs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Its ordinary sense is eager, desirous (see want); of a judge, a witness or an author, partial, inclined to one side. The adverb cupidē is “with bias” (M-O s.v. bias).
Classically a judgment given beforehand, a precedent, not a prejudice of the mind; the sense of harm to a case is legal and later. For prejudice, opīniō praejūdicāta.

phrases.latin: sine īrā et studiō, quōrum causās procul habeō
phrases.english: without anger or bias, whose causes I am far removed from

phrases.latin: postulō, ut nē quid hūc praejūdicātī afferātis
phrases.english: I ask you not to bring any preconceived opinion with you here

sources: Lewis & Short: studium · Lewis & Short: praejudico · Lewis & Short: cupidus · Lewis & Short: praejudicium
Tacitus from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-tacitus); the other passages as Lewis & Short quotes them.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. bias.
